title: Deduction, induction and abduction
note: A deductive argument aims to guarantee its conclusion: if the premises are true, the conclusion must be. An inductive argument aims only to make its conclusion probable, as when we generalize from a sample. Abduction, or inference to the best explanation, accepts the hypothesis that would best explain the evidence. Induction and abduction are ampliative and can be overturned by new evidence.

read.title: Three ways to reach a conclusion
text: Deduction aims at certainty. In a good deductive argument, the truth of the premises guarantees the truth of the conclusion: if all mammals breathe air and whales are mammals, whales breathe air. Nothing in the conclusion goes beyond what the premises already commit you to. That is also its limit: deduction unpacks information rather than adding new facts about the world.

Induction reaches further. From many observed cases we conclude something about unobserved ones: every swan Europeans had seen was white, so they concluded all swans were white. Such reasoning is ampliative, meaning its conclusion says more than its premises, and so it can fail. Black swans were found in Australia. A good inductive argument makes its conclusion probable, and more and better evidence can strengthen or weaken it.

Abduction, a term from Charles Sanders Peirce, is inference to the best explanation. A ball lies inside a room beneath a broken window, so you conclude someone threw or hit it through. You choose the hypothesis that would best explain the evidence, judging rivals by simplicity, how much they explain, and fit with what you already know. Scientists, mechanics, and detectives reason this way constantly, and like induction it can be overturned by new facts.

q.q: Why can inductive conclusions turn out false even from true premises?
o: They are ampliative: they say more than the premises
They always contain a formal fallacy

o: A ball beneath a broken window
